Written by the Vinaya-transmitting Śramaṇa Shuyu of Zhaokeng Temple in Ancient Hangzhou.
Regarding the Vinaya, it says: Once a śikṣamāṇā has completed her training in the precepts, she requests the bhikṣu-saṃgha to grant her the full ordination (mahā-śīla). This is as follows:

During the fourteen years following his attainment of the Way, he personally proclaimed the fourth of the Eight Rules of Respect for Mahāprajāpatī and others, ordaining them into the homeless life from his golden mouth.

Consequently, once a *śikṣamāṇā* has completed her training in the precepts, she must necessarily assemble a pure community of twenty monastics—both monks and nuns—to confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
If even one person is missing, the ritual procedure is not accomplished; the conferrer incurs an offense. This refers to the assembly.
The number was incomplete, as it could not cause the bhikṣuṇīs to give rise to the superior precepts (*adhiśīla*). Regarding those various ritual procedures, they were recorded in the Vinaya Piṭaka.
The Venerable Master Xuansu of Nanshan abridged the superfluous and extracted the essentials, compiling them as a manual for practice titled *Jisuji Jie mo* (Karmavācanā According to Circumstances).

To address its practical application, he further composed the *Shichao* (Manual of Matters) to fully explain its textual details. From the Tang dynasty until the present, more than a thousand years have passed. As for these matters...
The woodblocks for the *Chao* (Commentary) were lost; only the *Karmavācanā* (Ritual Procedures) remains, yet its practice is particularly difficult.

When my late teacher met the Old Master, he revived the traditions of both the ritual procedures (*zhi*) and their performance (*zuo*). He re-explained them, revealing their hidden meanings and adding ritual manuals (*yi*); thus, both principle and practice become clear.

In the spring of the Dingwei year, the nun-monk Mijiao of Kunshan, together with Lady Xu, ascended the mountain to offer a memorial feast, followed by a group of female disciples studying the precepts.
She came seeking full ordination (*upasampadā*). After practicing for half a month, she had gained a basic familiarity with the monastic protocols (*īryāpatha*).

First, the elder nun Mijiao was appointed as her preceptor (*upādhyāyī*); the nun Chaochen of Yangzhou served as the *karmakārikā*; the nun Yuanzheng of Zhenzhou served as the instructor (*śikṣamāṇācāryā*);

and nuns of esteemed virtue and seniority were selected to serve as the seven witnesses. Together with more than forty other nuns receiving ordination, she departed the boundary to travel south of the mountain.
Ye’an gathered the bhikṣuṇīs of that community and first conferred upon them the fundamental precepts. On the following day, the *upādhyāyī* struck the gavel to assemble the assembly;

after the formal announcement of the Tathāgata’s injunctions had been made, she led the nine masters on the altar and the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs up the mountain to request the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
The Elder [Master] then assembled the monks and nuns of both communities and performed the ritual for their complete ordination. This was the practice of the former Elder.

The "Two-Part Sangha" refers to the ritual for bestowing the precepts upon bhikṣuṇīs. Although I have not formally listed its procedures here, as I attended at the side of my predecessors, there was no dharma that did not pass before my eyes.
Since then, however, as the succession of teachers and disciples has not been continuous, the transmission has proceeded solely through the *bhikṣu* sangha.
This is because I originally looked up to the "dharma-milk" of the late Elder [Master]. Indeed, it is said that the conferral of the Dharma must accord with the capacities of those receiving it.
It is not possible to strive for this. Thus, those who received the precepts later on mostly did not have the opportunity to see it.

My dharma-nephew, Vinaya Master Songyin, emulating the lofty style of Shandao, exhorted others to cultivate pure deeds; when the conditions were ripe, his realization of the Way harmonized with the universe.
There was a nun named Heshang Juyuan, who was a dharma heir of the Venerable Zhen of Tanzhe. With a vajra-body, she fulfilled her steadfast vows;
practicing the dhūta ascetic disciplines, she shook off adventitious defilements. For thirty years, she remained as constant as a single day.
Her elder brother, the lay devotee Han Bingzhou, was a reincarnation of the Elder Sudatta and was profoundly faithful.
The Vinaya is the golden fortress of the Buddha-dharma. These two individuals both emerged from the gate of the Venerable Canglin.

Observing that Master Song’s every movement—whether coming or going, entering or exiting—never failed to accord with the monastic discipline (*vinaya*), they mobilized various patrons and donors to invite him to the Anāthapiṇḍika Monastery.

There he conferred the great precepts of the three ordination platforms (*tri-saṃvara*). The ordination site was exceptionally sublime, and every detail was magnificently adorned. The fourfold assembly gathered like clouds, exclaiming in admiration at such an unprecedented sight.

There was. After Master Song had conferred the *bhikṣu* precepts, he further commissioned the nun-monk Huiguanyuan as *upādhyāyī*, hoping that she would lead nine other nun-elders to form the two-fold assembly (*ubhayasaṃgha*) for the conferment of the *bhikṣuṇī* full ordination. Now, Master Song was the foremost disciple of my own master, Venerable Ding;
having served him for a long time and assisted him for many years, although I have not witnessed the conduct of his original teacher, [I know him well].
The dharma he performed was entirely in accord with the established regulations of my late Preceptor; could this not be an omen for his succession to the seat at Baohua?
In the winter of the Renwu year, the two masters Gju and Han came from the south to pay their respects to the Great Being of the Universal Gate (Avalokiteśvara).

They first arrived at Zhaokeng Temple to gaze upon and prostrate before the ancient Buddha’s ordination platform, where they inquired after him with great earnestness and fully recounted the aforementioned matters, expressing their deep longing for the late Elder.

Regarding the ritual procedures for ordination, I regret that I have not personally witnessed them. I request that you describe the ceremony for the conferral of precepts by the dual assembly of monks and nuns, so as to serve as a witness for future generations.
My intention is to enable the monastics who receive the full precepts—both monks and nuns—to behold together the sacred regulations of the Tathāgata and the rigorous discipline of the Vinaya.

Having exhorted you repeatedly and at length, I could not but comply with your request. Therefore, I have compiled into a single volume the ritual procedures I observed in years past for your perusal.

General Principles for the Ritual of Bestowing Precepts by the Two-Part Saṃgha (Twelve Rules) The Buddha ordained that when monks reside together, they must first establish a boundary (*sīmā*). If a boundary is not established, all ritual acts and other formal procedures will lack the efficacy of accomplishment, and the assembly of monks will incur offense.
Furthermore, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "By extension of this principle, the Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha may also establish its own boundary."
Regarding the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*):

because it protects the distinct assemblies, the ten masters of the two divisions must be strictly disciplined and act in accordance with the Dharma; they must be monks and nuns who understand the Vinaya, rather than merely fulfilling a required number.
The presiding master of the Dharma should first carefully evaluate them.

The administrative officers of the two divisions each have their respective jurisdictions; they should not be intermingled. When a nun bestows the fundamental dharma, she employs only the nuns' officials.
Upon reaching the assembly of great monks, the bhikṣus shall then manage the proceedings.

Regarding the two-part conferral of the precepts, the primary authority rests with the Bhikṣu-saṃgha. The Bhikṣuṇīs receive the fundamental dharma, both parties adhering to the ritual procedures of the Bhikṣu-saṃgha;
they must not follow worldly practices, as doing so would contravene the Buddha’s regulations.
When a bhikṣuṇī receives the full ordination (mahā-śīla), it must take place within the assembly of both orders (ubhayasaṃgha) for it to be in accordance with the Dharma.

First, she must undergo a thorough examination within her own order, perform repentance, and be granted the ten branches or the six dharmas of the precepts. Having purified her training and generated a superior resolve (adhimukti-citta), she may proceed.
Next, the fundamental precepts are conferred. Thereafter, one requests the full ordination (*upasampadā*) from the community of bhikṣus, thereby entering the ranks of the Triple Gem.
Although many nowadays receive [ordination] through expedient means, one must nonetheless understand that the Vinaya laws are strictly rigorous.
As clarified in the Vinaya, it is impossible for one who has not received the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇerī to receive full ordination (upasampadā).
Therefore, the term "śrāmaṇerī" is repeated in the text to demonstrate that the stages of practice are not to be confused.

In the original *Duyoushijiefa* (The Ritual for Bestowing the Precepts Individually), the word "equal" (*deng*) did not exist. When three people were on a single altar, it was termed a "multitude," which was difficult to manage;
therefore, the word "equal" was added to include the other two persons.

When a *bhikṣuṇī* bestows the precepts upon another *bhikṣuṇī*, she must inquire regarding the prohibitions (*antarāyika-dharma*) in private; however, when a *bhikṣu* bestows the precepts upon a *bhikṣuṇī*, he is not permitted to inquire about such difficulties in private, but only to do so before the ten masters on the ordination platform.
This dharma-karman is merely a preparatory rite; it is not yet the time for the formal proclamation of the precepts. Therefore, the characteristics of the precepts are not declared.
There are two reasons for this: first, because it is not the actual conferral of full ordination; second, because the assembly of the two divisions of the Saṃgha does not consist of twenty members.
The precepts are conferred within the assembly of great bhikṣus. She is called a *dharmabhikṣuṇī* (a nun of the fundamental dharma) so that her position in the hierarchy is not neglected;
she is not called a *śrāmaṇerikā* because she has already received the fundamental dharma; and she is not called a *bhikṣuṇī* because she has not yet obtained the full ordination (*mahā-śīla*).
The Vinaya rules were established by the Tathāgata; these invocations are the regulations for gathering the assembly.
All titles are written in large characters at the top of the line, while the ritual texts are indented one character to facilitate reading.

The Vinaya permits the conferral of full ordination (*upasampadā*) in frontier regions with a quorum of fewer than half the two assemblies, because it is difficult to assemble the full community of monks there.
The ritual procedures for receiving ordination are no different from those prescribed here.

Once the *upādhyāya* has granted permission, he first appoints ten masters from the community of nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*). Regarding these ten masters of the nun’s community...)

Thereafter, they exit the boundary (*sīmā*) to perform the ritual procedures. Upon arriving at the designated hall, they must practice the rites according to the Dharma until they are thoroughly proficient in their sequence.
The Rector (*karmadāna*) shall have the ordination platform (*dīkṣā-maṇḍala*) swept and cleaned; if no such platform exists, one must be constructed.
At the upper center, the principal seat is established. To the right of the seat, a small table is placed. In the center, the second seat is laid out.

The remaining eight seats are arranged in four on the left and four on the right, facing one another. On the day of receiving full ordination, banners, streamers, precious canopies, and necklaces are suspended.
Directly beneath the altar, a single incense table is set up, where candles are lit and flowers are offered. Furthermore, in a screened-off area, a single interrogation station is established.

The Method for Assembling the Congregation by Striking the Gavel Twice: First, one should not occupy a small seat; next, one should request the precepts and perform the *kṣamā* (confession). Once the response has been received and one is pure and untainted, one awaits the opportunity to ascend the platform.

The Ritual for Praying for the Emperor’s Longevity (Based on the Ancient Altar Rites). At the commencement of ascending the altar, there is a specific section for praying for longevity. This is because the Sangha’s propagation of the Buddha-Dharma necessarily relies upon external protection;
thus, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, the World-Honored One once gave his formal entrustment. Should one violate the Buddha’s words and fail the state...
The Master said: "I fear that the propagation of the teachings may be difficult. For now, we shall continue to follow the ritual protocols of the ancient altar.
The *vīnāyaka* shall chant the *brahman* and intone the 'Prayers for the Longevity of the Sovereign' and the incense hymns, with the entire assembly joining in harmony."

devas coming, nāgas coming, and spirits coming to make offerings to me—these are not bhikṣuṇīs, nor are they daughters of the Śākya clan.
Within this, for as long as life lasts, you must not commit any violation. Can you uphold them? (She answers: I can uphold them.

Fifth: One must not engage in physical contact, even with an animal. If a bhikṣuṇī, with a defiled mind, engages in physical contact with a man who has a defiled mind—below the armpits and above the knees—whether by pressing or rubbing; [she commits an offense].
Whether pulling, pushing, stroking against the grain, stroking with the grain, lifting up, lowering down, grasping, or pressing firmly—this is not a bhikṣuṇī;
this is not a daughter of the Śākya clan. You must not violate this for as long as you live. Can you uphold it? (Answer:
I can uphold it.
Sixth: One must not commit eight matters, even with an animal.

If a bhikṣuṇī, with a man who has a defiled mind, takes his hand, takes his robe, enters a secluded place, stands together with him, speaks together with him, walks together with him, touches his body, or makes an appointment with him.
If one commits these eight matters, one is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, nor a daughter of the Śākya clan, because of having committed these eight matters.
Regarding these, you must not commit them for as long as life lasts. Can you maintain this? (Answer: I can maintain it.
Seventh: One must not conceal the offenses of others, even those as minor as *dukkaṭa* or *dubbhāsita*.
If a bhikṣuṇī knows that another bhikṣuṇī has committed a *pārājika* offense, yet does not herself raise it, nor inform the Saṃgha or a group of many [monks].

Later, at another time, if this bhikṣuṇī has left the religious life, or has been expelled, or is barred from participating in the affairs of the Saṃgha, or has entered a non-Buddhist sect, she should then say: "I already knew that such and such things existed;
she was not a bhikṣuṇī, nor was she a daughter of the Śākyas, because she concealed a grave offense. Regarding this matter, you must not [associate with her] for as long as you live.
[If] one commits [an offense], can you maintain [the precept]? (Answer: I can maintain it.
Eighth: One must not follow a monk who has been formally accused, nor even a park keeper or a novice (śrāmaṇera), nor a nun (bhikṣuṇī).
If a nun knows that a bhikṣu has been formally accused by the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s instructions,

yet he does not comply and does not confess while the Saṃgha has not yet granted him reinstatement, and she nevertheless associates with him, that nun should be admonished by the other nuns as follows:
"Sister, do you know? The Saṃgha has now formally charged this bhikṣu in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching.
He does not comply and does not repent; the Saṃgha has not yet granted him formal co-residence. You must not follow him.

When that bhikṣuṇī thus admonishes the other bhikṣuṇī, if she persists and does not relinquish her position, that bhikṣuṇī shall be admonished up to three times so that she may abandon this matter. Only then...

Up to the third admonition: if she relinquishes [the offense], it is well; if she does not relinquish it, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, nor a daughter of the Śākya clan, because she has followed [the path of] suspension.
Regarding this matter, you must not commit an offense for as long as life lasts. Can you maintain this? (Answer: I can maintain it.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: After the eight heavy offenses (*aṣṭau pārājikāḥ*) have been explained, four similes are taught in summary.
One should address them as follows: "Listen, daughter of noble family! The Tathāgata, the Arhat, has already expounded the eight *pārājika* rules and has further taught four analogies.
If one commits any of the eight heavy offenses, it is like severing a person's head; they can never be restored to life again. It is also like cutting down a *tāla* tree."
The mind will no longer grow or develop. It is like a needle with a broken eye, which can no longer be used;
or like a large stone split into two parts, which cannot be joined back together. If a bhikṣuṇī commits one of the eight grave offenses, she cannot again achieve the conduct of a bhikṣuṇī.
You must not commit any of these for as long as you live. Can you maintain this? (Answer: I can maintain it.
Seventeenth: The Subsequent Explanation of the Four Reliances (Furthermore, one should say):
"Listen, daughter of good family. The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has taught the four reliances.
By relying upon these, a bhikṣuṇī may go forth, receive full ordination, and fulfill the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī."
First: A bhikṣuṇī relies on rag-robes (pāṃsukūla) to go forth and receive full ordination, thereby perfecting the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī.
Can you maintain this for as long as life lasts? (Answer: I can maintain it.
If one obtains long-term benefits, such as robes offered by a donor or robes made from cut and mended cloth, one may accept them.
Second: A bhikṣuṇī relies on the alms bowl for begging food; having gone forth and received the full precepts, she fulfills the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī.
"Can you maintain this throughout your entire life? (She replies: "I can maintain it."
If one obtains long-term benefits, or food assigned by the Saṃgha, or food sent by a donor, or food on the eighth day of the month, or food on the fourteenth day, or food on the fifteenth day,
or food on the first day of the month, or the regular food of the community of monks, or food offered by a donor’s invitation, these should be accepted.
Third: A bhikṣuṇī may dwell under a tree, go forth into homelessness, receive the full precepts, and thus perfect the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī.
Are you able to maintain this for as long as life lasts? (Answer: I am able to maintain it.
If one obtains long-term benefits, such as a separate room, a pointed-roofed house, a small room, a stone chamber, or two rooms with a single door, these may be accepted.
Fourth, a bhikṣuṇī who relies on medicinal drugs that have become decomposed may go forth and receive full ordination, thereby perfecting the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī.
"Can you maintain this throughout your entire life? (He replies: "I can maintain it.
"If you obtain long-term benefits—ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, or rock sugar—you should accept them."
In the Vinaya, because a bhikṣuṇī was dwelling alone in an araṇya and a difficult situation arose, the Buddha had already prohibited sitting under trees.
That the old text is still cited here is to enable her to understand the four reliances (catvāri niśrayāḥ).
The three of you have completed the reception of the full ordination (*upasampadā*). The *jñapti-caturtha-karman* has been accomplished in accordance with the Dharma.

You have obtained a proper place of residence. Your preceptor (*upādhyāya*) is in accordance with the Dharma; your instructors (*ācārya*) are in accordance with the Dharma. The two divisions of the Saṃgha are fully complete. You should properly receive the teachings and instructions.

One should exhort others to cultivate merit, repair stupas, and make offerings to the Sangha. One must not disobey any instruction given by one’s preceptor (upādhyāya) or teacher (ācārya) that is in accordance with the Dharma.
One should study, inquire, and recite the sūtras, diligently seeking skillful means within the Buddha-dharma.
One attains the fruit of *srotāpanna*, the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, the fruit of *anāgāmin*, and the fruit of *arhat*.
Your initial resolve to leave the household life has not been in vain; its fruition shall never cease. As for other matters you do not yet know, you should inquire of your *upādhyāya* and *ācārya*.
Having finished the prostrations and risen from your seat, proceed to the hall to pay homage to the Buddha.

(The newly ordained monks hold their implements; proceeding from the southwest corner to the rear of the altar and descending, they receive [the precepts] in this same order at the second altar, and so on through to the final altar).
The Preceptor says:
"The conferral of the precepts is now complete. The assembly chants the Buddha’s name in unison and performs the dedication of merit.
(The newly ordained monks descend from the platform with their ritual implements; the ten masters for the nuns first descend from their seats and take their positions).
The Ritual for the Eighteenth Dedication of Merit and Departure from the Altar: The Master of Ceremonies says:

"All shall stand in a single row facing upward. Upon hearing the sound of the chime, prostrate three times. After rising from the prostrations, adjust your robes, rise to a kneeling position, inquire after one another’s well-being, and then separate into rows."
(The nine masters on the altar are arranged in two rows: five in front and four behind. The ten nuns’ masters are also arranged in rows facing upward:
one in front and nine behind. After performing three prostrations—or one—facing upward and completing the inquiry of courtesy, the ten nuns’ masters withdraw beneath the eaves.
The ten masters on the altar then proceed last, descending the right-hand steps from the altar and circumambulating toward the northeast.)
Upon reaching the front of the altar, the first master leads the first group; the nine masters follow next; and the bhikṣuṇīs, led by the tenth master, follow after them.
The *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable) recites the verse:
The supreme practice of the merit of receiving the precepts— I dedicate all boundless and excellent blessings (the Master performs one prostration together).
May all sentient beings submerged in suffering Swiftly proceed to the Buddha-field of Amitābha (as before).
All Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, And all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas (as before).
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra (Section on the Twenty Preceptors’ Inquiries and the Formation of Opposing Lines):
The *Upādhyāya* turns to face south and stands. The two *Ācāryas* who lead the ceremony first escort the newly ordained [monks] at the rear;

once the newly ordained have completed their procession, the ten *Ācāryas* of the *Bhikṣuṇīs* take the lead from behind. The nine *Ācāryas* of the *Mahāsāṃghika* monks likewise take the lead from behind.

Continuing from above: The ritual attendants strike the *yin-qing* (leading chime) twice and precede the Abbot. The newly ordained monks arrive before the Abbot’s quarters and kneel in two rows facing each other with palms joined.
They remain there until all the masters have passed by, at which point they rise and proceed in two rows to the ranks before the Abbot. The Abbot faces south;
the nineteen masters line up facing him and perform three prostrations—or one—spreading their hands in the "eight-character" (*ba-zi*) position.
[The ceremony] begins. The attendant calls out:

"All, line up facing upward. Upon hearing the sound of the *qing* (stone chime), perform three prostrations with palms joined in gratitude [the Master joins his palms]. After the prostrations, lift the robes and rise.
After the formal inquiries have been completed and the assembly has divided into groups, the Abbot enters his room.
The various masters disperse. Once the newly ordained monks have performed their prostrations of gratitude to the Master of Ceremonies, they then return to the hall in proper order.

Postscript: This ritual appears extremely simple when observed on the surface; yet, its actual implementation is truly difficult. Unless one possesses great spiritual capacity (*mahā-indriya*), it cannot be attained.
Those with the power of great patience cannot believe in this Dharma. The Buddha said that women are delusive and confused, possessing many afflictions;
they may give rise to anger, thereby obstructing diligent practice, or they may give rise to pride, thereby obstructing the proper transmission and reception of the teachings according to the Dharma.

Thus, these afflictions delude the field of the mind and obstruct the Noble Path. For this reason, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, the Buddha’s maternal aunt, together with five hundred women of the Śākya clan, went to the gate of the Jetavana monastery seeking ordination. The Buddha did not grant her permission.

Mahāprajāpatī and the others walked until their feet were cracked and their bodies were covered in dust; weeping in sorrow, they would not leave. Seeing them, Ānanda felt compassion and [petitioned the Buddha] three times.

She requested the Tathāgata. Out of compassion for her, the Buddha established the Eight Rules of Respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*), saying: "If you can observe and practice these for as long as you live, I shall permit you to go forth. Ānanda transmitted this instruction accordingly.
Mahāprajāpatī and the others replied three times, accepting it upon their heads and vowing to practice it. Thus, the community of nuns was established from that point on.

Later, the rule was established that both monks and nuns must receive full ordination through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations). Therefore, the *Śāstra* says: "By means of the nuns..."
By equally practicing the Eightfold Respectful Observances (*aṣṭa-guru-dharma*), one can ensure that the True Dharma of the Tathāgata does not decline. Alas!

In the age of the Final Dharma, nuns who receive the precepts are as numerous as sesame seeds or millet; yet if one seeks even a single person who understands the Eightfold Respectful Observances, such a one is still unattainable, let alone one who actually practices them.
The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature. Those who possess Buddha-nature shall all attain Buddhahood."
The Buddha’s *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Although all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature, it must be through the observance of the precepts that it is subsequently seen.
It further states: "A woman who attains the Buddha-nature becomes a 'great man' among women. Now, Master Juyuan is precisely such a person;
he is able to practice the Eight Respects and relies upon Vinaya masters, while also living together with his elder brother Hanping Zhou.
Gentlemen, I request that you continue this ritual by offering pears and jujubes. I know that the two of you would not do so for your own sake;

rather, you wish for everyone to receive and transmit [the teachings] according to the Dharma, thereby ensuring that the Vinaya endures for a long time. This heart of yours toward the Dharma shall surely remain imperishable together.
On the second day of the second month, I set down my brush; thus, this postscript.
